items.question: How do you understand the contrast between how quickly you learn something and how quickly you use it?
items.object: His contrast between learning slowly and applying knowledge quickly
items.answer: For example, when other people were doing mental-arithmetic problems in second grade and might have only gotten halfway through, I would already be done. It was the kind of thing that required no conscious thought. In today’s fashionable terminology, maybe System 1: it goes directly through surface-level consciousness, you look at it once and the answer comes out. That gave me a great sense of accomplishment from doing math problems, because I felt I was actually comparatively slow at learning things. How should I put it? For example, when I read a section of code, I need much more time than other people to understand the whole thing—the whole content, the whole context. But once I understand it, I use it very quickly.

items.question: How did your sense that you needed more time to learn shape your approach to studying?

items.answer: Before sleeping, I would try every possible way until I could recite it all, haltingly. Even if there were many pauses, as long as I could recall it, that was fine. Then I would sleep, and wake up the next day able to recite it fluently forwards and backwards. My thinking at the time was that, because I needed more time, I needed to learn things earlier than others. By the second year of middle school, I had already worked through all of high school, and in the third year I began learning calculus.
